core.text: A wish is **utinam + subjunctive (the 'if only …' wish; the tense says whether it can still come true)**. *Utinam veniat!* — may he come, if only he comes (still possible: present subjunctive). *Utinam venīret!* — if only he were coming (he isn't: imperfect subjunctive). *Utinam vēnisset!* — if only he had come (he didn't: pluperfect subjunctive). The negative is *utinam nē*. Latin name: *coniūnctīvus optātīvus cum utinam*.
English: *may you be happy* (possible); *if only I were rich* (I'm not); *if only I had known* (I didn't). English also steps back in time to say 'impossible': *were*, *had*.
utinam (nē) + present = a hope; + imperfect = an impossible wish about now; + pluperfect = an impossible wish about the past.

invented.en: If only I were with you!

core.text: The same imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive appear in 'if I were …, I would …' sentences. The difference is *utinam* (or a bare wish) against *sī* plus a second clause that draws the consequence: *utinam Rōmae essem* (wish) but *sī Rōmae essem, laetus essem* (condition).

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *vīvāmus, amēmus* (let us live, let us love) and *valeat* (may he fare well) are wishes and exhortations in the present subjunctive without *utinam*. *Utinam* only makes the wish explicit; the imperfect and pluperfect never appear in the 'let us / let him' type.

The learner's notes (Week 33, 'Contrafactual Optative'): a present optative is a wish about the future that is technically possible even if unlikely (*amīcī veniant!* would that my friends came!); an imperfect optative is a wish about the present that is contrary to fact, and *utinam* is used especially then (*utinam ambulāre possem!* would that I could walk!; *utinam tempus esset discēdendī!*); a pluperfect optative is a contrary-to-fact wish about the past (*utinam numquam nātus essem!*, *utinam nē vēnissem!*).

Softer wishes use *velim* (I would like) and *vellem* (I wish, I would have liked): *vellem sī magis esset anus* — I'd wish it, if she were more of an old woman (Martial, Week 14). Ørberg's chapter 32 gives Medus's *utinam salvī in Graeciam perveniant!* and Lydia's *utinam aliquandō līber patriam videam!*; chapter 33 turns to the impossible: *utinam ego Rōmae essem!*
